questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD skills: PVCs, InitContainers, ConfigMaps, sidecars, readiness/liveness, and network policies in a realistic static content scenario.

Key Concepts
- PVC-backed volumes and ConfigMap mounts
- InitContainer for initial bootstrap
- Sidecar for live file reloads
- ConfigMap-driven content flags
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress control

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: static-content-server
  namespace: ckad-demo
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: static-content
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: static-content
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: html
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: static-content-pvc
        - name: template
          configMap:
            name: page-template
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: page-config
      initContainers:
        - name: init
          image: alpine
          command: ["sh", "-c", "cp /template/index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: html
              mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
            - name: template
              mountPath: /template
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:alpine
          volumeMounts:
            - name: html
              mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
        - name: reload-agent
          image: busybox
          command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do inotifywait -e modify /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html; nginx -s reload; done"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: html
              mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /index.html
          port: 80
        initialDelaySeconds: 5
        periodSeconds: 10
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /index.html
          port: 80
        initialDelaySeconds: 15
        periodSeconds: 20
```

Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle multi-namespace isolation if the same config is needed across namespaces?
- What changes if you switch to an A/B testing banner using two ConfigMaps and a canary rollout?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates practical CKAD skills including per-namespace configuration management, InitContainer usage, sidecar patterns, secure secret handling, and network policy implementation.

## Key Concepts
- Per-namespace deployments with shared persistent volumes
- InitContainer for runtime dependency installation
- Inotify-based file change detection and yamllint validation
- In-service reload capabilities (nginx -s reload)
- ConfigMap and Secret integration patterns
- TLS sidecar implementation for secure communications
- Namespace-level NetworkPolicy for egress restrictions

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton of the Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: config-watcher
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: config-watcher
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: config-watcher
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
        image: alpine:latest
        command: ['sh', '-c', 'apk add --no-cache inotify-tools yamllint']
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:alpine
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config-pvc
          mountPath: /config/dynamic
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
      - name: config-watcher
        image: alpine:latest
        command: ['sh', '-c', 'while inotifywait -e modify /config/dynamic/*.yaml; do yamllint /config/dynamic/*.yaml && nginx -s reload; done']
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config-pvc
          mountPath: /config/dynamic
        env:
        - name: STATUS_URL
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: status-secret
              key: url
      - name: tls-sidecar
        image: envoyproxy/envoy:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8443
      volumes:
      - name: config-pvc
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: config-pvc
      - name: nginx-defaults
        configMap:
          name: nginx-defaults
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: config-pvc
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: nginx-defaults
  namespace: target-namespace
data:
  nginx.conf: |
    # Default Nginx configuration
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: status-secret
  namespace: target-namespace
type: Opaque
data:
  url: aHR0cDovL3N0YXR1cy5sb2NhbC9hcGkvdjEvcmVsb2Fk
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: config-watcher-netpol
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: config-watcher
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: internal-services
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
```

## Trade-offs
- **Inotify vs polling**: Inotify is more efficient but requires file system support
- **Sidecar overhead**: TLS sidecar adds complexity and resource usage
- **Single namespace scope**: Limited to namespace-level isolation vs cluster-wide
- **PVC dependency**: Requires storage management and backup strategies
- **Container sharing**: Process communication within pod vs separate services

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design a scheduled, idempotent data archival workflow using core Kubernetes primitives (CronJob, PVCs, ConfigMap, InitContainer, HTTP post, probes) with practical considerations for reliability (backoff, history limits) and operations (PDB).

## Key Concepts
- CronJob scheduling and job lifecycles
- PVC data/input and output destinations
- InitContainer usage for tooling installation
- ConfigMap-driven thresholds and defaults
- Resource requests/limits, probes, backoff, and RBAC considerations
- PodDisruptionBudget applicability to ephemeral batch workloads

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton patch (CronJob)
apiVersion: batch/v1beta1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: data-archiver
  namespace: nightly-backups
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 3
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: archiver
            image: my-registry/archiver:latest
            volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
            - name: backups
              mountPath: /backups
            resources:
              requests:
                cpu: "100m"
                memory: "128Mi"
              limits:
                cpu: "500m"
                memory: "256Mi"
            command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "/usr/local/bin/archiver.sh"]
            readinessProbe:
              exec:
                command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "test -d /data && true"]
              initialDelaySeconds: 10
              periodSeconds: 30
            livenessProbe:
              exec:
                command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "test -f /backups/backup-*.tar.gz || true"]
              initialDelaySeconds: 30
              periodSeconds: 60
          volumes:
          - name: data
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: data-pvc
          - name: backups
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: backups-pvc
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
        
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test behavior when backup-config DAYs_OLDER changes in-flight?
- How would you rollback a failed run and protect against partial backups?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests CKAD mastery of multi-resource coordination, init containers, volumes, secrets, and network policies. It also validates per-namespace config management and safe log persistence.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob and Job orchestration across a namespace
- InitContainer to install client tooling and share /tools
- ConfigMap and Secret usage for migrations and DB credentials
- PVC-backed /logs for auditability
- NetworkPolicy restricting egress to Postgres
- Status tracking in a namespace ConfigMap

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: db-migrate
spec:
  schedule: "*/12 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          volumes:
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: logs-pvc
          - name: migrations
            configMap:
              name: migrations-config
          - name: tools
            emptyDir: {}
          initContainers:
          - name: installer
            image: alpine:3.18
            command: ["sh","-c","apk add --no-cache postgresql-client && mkdir -p /tools && cp /usr/bin/psql /tools/psql"]
            volumeMounts:
            - name: tools
              mountPath: /tools
          containers:
          - name: migrate
            image: migrate-base:latest
            command: ["/tools/psql","-h","$(DB_HOST)","-U","$(DB_USER)","-d","$(DB_NAME)","-f","/migrations/*.sql"]
            envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: db-credentials
            - configMapRef:
                name: db-config
            volumeMounts:
            - name: migrations
              mountPath: /migrations
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Trade-offs
- InitContainer size vs main image size; tooling duplication
- Per-namespace migrations risk drift vs centralized control
- Secret rotation complexity; ensure timely updates
- Logging volume retention vs cost

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This checks secure defaults and practical CKAD patterns: ConfigMap/Secret usage, correct SecurityContext, and health checks.

## Key Concepts
- SecurityContext: runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, readOnlyRootFilesystem, capabilities: drop: ALL
- ConfigMap and Secret mounting into containers
- Resource requests/limits
- Liveness and readiness probes
- ClusterIP service exposure

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal Deployment skeleton (yaml)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: flask-app
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: flask-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: flask-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: flask
        image: python:3.11-slim
        command: ["python", "/app/main.py"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: app-config
          mountPath: /app/config
        - name: api-key
          mountPath: /secrets
          readOnly: true
        securityContext:
          runAsUser: 1001
          runAsNonRoot: true
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"]
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 5000
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 5000
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "200m"
            memory: "256Mi"
      volumes:
      - name: app-config
        configMap:
          name: flask-config
      - name: api-key
        secret:
          secretName: flask-api-key
```

```yaml
# Minimal Service skeleton
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: flask-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: flask-app
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 5000
  type: ClusterIP
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you rotate the API_KEY secret without downtime?
- What are the trade-offs of using readOnlyRootFilesystem in production?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design per-namespace automation for safe, auditable canary rollouts with minimal disruption. It emphasizes idempotence, config-driven behavior, and secure traffic controls.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob scope and schedule
- Namespace-scoped ConfigMaps and Secrets interplay
- InitContainers for tool provisioning
- Patch strategy for container images (kubectl patch, jq)
- Logs via PVC and heartbeat-status tracking
- NetworkPolicy least privilege in a per-namespace context

## Code Example
```javascript
# Minimal CronJob skeleton (yaml shown as JS block per guidelines)
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: canary-roller
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  schedule: "*/5 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: install-tools
            image: alpine:3.18
            command: ["sh","-c","apk add --no-cache curl jq kubectl"]
          containers:
          - name: canary-roller
            image: registry.example/canary-roller:latest
            command: ["sh","-c","/scripts/canary-roll.sh"]
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          volumes:
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: canary-logs
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you guard against partial failures when some Deployments succeed and others fail during a run?
- What RBAC changes would you add to restrict the CronJob's patch actions to only image fields?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical Kubernetes hardening: securityContext at both pod and container levels, probes that reflect real app health, and a deterministic rolling update trigger. It also checks how to verify and rollback in a live system.

## Key Concepts

## Why This Is Asked

## Key Concepts
- Container SecurityContext: runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, readOnlyRootFilesystem for container isolation

- PodDisruptionBudget: maintain minimum healthy pods during maintenance
- Rollout and rollback procedures for safe deployments

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-gateway
  labels:
    app: api-gateway
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api-gateway
    spec:
      securityContext:
        fsGroup: 1001
      containers:
      - name: api-gateway
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          runAsUser: 10001
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          capabilities:
            drop:
            - "ALL"
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /srv
        - name: config
          mountPath: /etc/app
      volumes:
      - name: data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: api-gateway-pvc

          name: api-gateway-config
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: api-gateway-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:

```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design production-ready batch workloads in Kubernetes, including secure configuration management, job lifecycle controls, and deployment strategies for config-driven restarts.

## Key Concepts
- **concurrencyPolicy: Forbid** - Prevents overlapping job executions, ensuring data consistency
- **backoffLimit: 3** - Limits retry attempts for failed pods before marking the job as failed
- **ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 86400** - Auto-cleansup completed jobs after 24 hours
- **successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3** - Retains recent successful job history for debugging/auditing
- **checksum annotation** - Triggers pod recreation when ConfigMap/Secret changes (requires script to generate hash)
- **envFrom** - Mounts all ConfigMap/Secret values as environment variables without explicit key mapping

## Verification Under Simulated Load
1. **Test concurrency**: Trigger manual job while another runs - should fail with "Cannot determine if job needs to be started"
2. **Test failure handling**: Set invalid config, verify backoff retries 3 times
3. **Test cleanup**: Check completed jobs are removed after 24h TTL

## Verification On Config Change
1. Update ConfigMap: `kubectl apply -f analytics-config.yaml`
2. Verify annotation checksum updates in next job
3. Confirm new pod picks up new environment variables
4. Use `kubectl get pods` to verify new pod creation timestamp

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD skills around in-cluster tooling, Pod security checks, and non-intrusive governance in a namespace-scoped pattern. It avoids admission webhooks and reinforces RBAC, Secrets, PVCs, InitContainers, and NetworkPolicies.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped Deployment pattern without admission controllers
- SecurityContext defaults: non-root, readOnlyRootFilesystem, runAsUser
- Secret-backed Bearer token for API calls and in-cluster service accounts
- Logs persisted to a PVC; InitContainer for curl/jq
- Readiness/Liveness probes and a strict egress policy via NetworkPolicy

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: compliance-guard
  namespace: your-namespace
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: compliance-guard
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: compliance-guard
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: init-tools
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq > /dev/null 2>&1 || true"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
      containers:
        - name: guard
          image: your-registry/compliance-guard:latest
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: compliance-token
          env:
            - name: PORTAL_URL
              value: "http://compliance-portal:8080"
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while true; do ./guard --check-pod-security; sleep 60; done"]
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            runAsUser: 1000
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
        
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
      volumes:
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: logs-pvc
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          spreadConstraintLabelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: compliance-guard
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Question Is Asked

This question evaluates a candidate's ability to design production-ready, per-namespace observability data flows—a critical skill for platform engineers and SREs. It tests familiarity with Kubernetes security primitives, resource management, and operational patterns that generic deployments often overlook.

## Key Concepts Tested

- **Per-namespace isolation:** Scoping a Deployment to each namespace ensures data locality and prevents cross-namespace metric contamination.
- **PVC-backed data flow:** Tailing from a PVC provides durability and allows pods to restart without data loss.
- **Security hardening:** NetworkPolicies, Secrets, and resource limits demonstrate a defense-in-depth approach.
- **Operational concerns:** Probes, InitContainers, and sidecars reflect real-world operational complexity.

## Common Pitfalls

Candidates often miss NetworkPolicy egress rules, underconfigure resource limits, or overlook the trade-offs between Pushgateway reliability and simplicity. Strong candidates will proactively discuss alternatives like Prometheus scraping or distributed tracing backends.

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD orchestration across multiple resources: per-namespace autonomy, lifecycle cleanup, and secure external reporting. It evaluates understanding of CronJob scope, ConfigMaps for TTL, Secrets, and network isolation.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob per-namespace scope and cross-resource cleanup
- TTL-driven lifecycle logic for PVCs and Jobs
- Logs and digest state via PVC and ConfigMap
- InitContainer for kubectl/jq, Secrets for API keys
- TLS sidecar, readiness/liveness probes
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricting egress

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: namespace-cleanup
spec:
  schedule: "*/30 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: cleanup-sa
          containers:
          - name: cleanup
            image: my-registry/cleanup:latest
            command: ["/bin/sh","-c","/cleanup/cleanup.sh"]
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          volumes:
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: logs-pvc
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test TTL boundaries and idempotency of deletions?
- What RBAC and admission controls are essential for this pattern?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design a periodic batch using CronJob with PV, ConfigMap-driven config, Secrets, and RBAC, plus resiliency and rollback.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob vs Job, ConfigMap, Secret, PersistentVolumeClaim, RBAC
- startingDeadlineSeconds, backoffLimit, preStop lifecycle
- readinessProbe and livenessProbe, serviceAccount scope

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: daily-processor
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 3600
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 3
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: batch-job-sa
          volumes:
          - name: data-pvc
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: data-pvc
          containers:
          - name: daily-processor
            image: batch-processor:latest
            volumeMounts:
            - name: data-pvc
              mountPath: /data
            envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: cron-config
            env:
            - name: API_KEY
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: api-credentials
                  key: API_KEY
            readinessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /health
                port: 8080
              initialDelaySeconds: 10
              periodSeconds: 30
            livenessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /ready
                port: 8080
              initialDelaySeconds: 30
              periodSeconds: 30
            lifecycle:
              preStop:
                exec:
                  command: ["sh","-c","sleep 5"]
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you monitor backlog and guarantee idempotent processing across restarts?
- How would you rollback a broken patch to a previous CronJob manifest?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests the ability to compose a production-ready backup workflow using core Kubernetes primitives (CronJob, Secret, ConfigMap, PVC, NetworkPolicy) while understanding scope, lifecycle management, and security boundaries.

## Key Concepts
- **CronJob per-namespace scope**: Each namespace runs its own backup Job, ensuring isolation and scope-bound retention
- **InitContainer**: Installs mysqldump and gzip tools at Pod startup before the backup container runs
- **Secrets and ConfigMaps**: Store database credentials securely and retention policies as configuration
- **PVC-backed storage**: Provides persistent storage for backup files independent of Pod lifecycle
- **Probes**: Readiness and liveness probes ensure backup reliability and Pod health
- **NetworkPolicy**: Restricts egress traffic at the namespace level to prevent data exfiltration

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: ns-backup
  namespace: my-namespace
spec:
  schedule: "0 */6 * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: installer
            image: debian:latest
            command: ["sh", "-c", "apt-get update && apt-get install -y mysql-client gzip"]
            volumeMounts:
            - name: backup-volume
              mountPath: /backups
          containers:
          - name: backup
            image: alpine:latest
            command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
            args:
            - |
              mysqldump -h $DB_HOST -u $DB_USER -p$DB_PASSWORD $DB_NAME | gzip > /backups/$DATE.sql.gz
              find /backups -name "*.sql.gz" -mtime +$RETENTION_DAYS -delete
            env:
            - name: DB_HOST
              value: "localhost"
            - name: DB_USER
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: db-creds
                  key: username
            - name: DB_PASSWORD
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: db-creds
                  key: password
            - name: DB_NAME
              value: "appdb"
            - name: DATE
              value: "$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
            - name: RETENTION_DAYS
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef:
                  name: backup-config
                  key: retentionDays
            volumeMounts:
            - name: backup-volume
              mountPath: /backups
            readinessProbe:
              exec:
                command: ["ls", "/backups"]
              initialDelaySeconds: 5
              periodSeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              exec:
                command: ["ls", "/backups"]
              initialDelaySeconds: 15
              periodSeconds: 20
          volumes:
          - name: backup-volume
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: backup-pvc
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Trade-offs
- **PVC vs. emptyDir**: PVC provides persistence across Pod restarts but requires pre-provisioned storage; emptyDir is simpler but loses data on Pod termination
- **InitContainer vs. multi-stage image**: InitContainer adds startup overhead; a custom multi-stage image is leaner but requires image maintenance
- **Per-namespace CronJob**: Simplifies scope and retention per namespace but increases operational overhead compared to a centralized cluster-wide solution
- **NetworkPolicy**: Enhances security but requires careful planning of allowed egress rules to avoid breaking legitimate traffic
